name: Slow cinema
summary: A cinema of duration. Few cuts, a still or slow camera, ordinary tasks shown in real time and little plot. The viewer's attention does the work that the cut usually does.

philosophy.core_thesis: Time is the material of film, so a shot is held until the viewer sees the place and the person and feels the hours pass.
design_principles: Hold each shot for 30 to 180 s and cut at an average shot length of 30 s or more, with a whole scene in one take.
Lock the camera on a tripod, or move it at a walking pace of 0.2 to 0.5 m/s along a path that the person sets.
Frame in a wide shot with 40% to 70% of the picture left to a landscape, a room or a sky, and keep the person at 10% to 30% of the height.
Use the available light, a key-to-fill ratio of 2:1 or lower, with long daylight shots from dawn to dusk.
Shoot ordinary work, such as a walk, a meal or a wait, in real time and leave no plot reason for it.
Record the sound of the place, with wind, rain and an engine, at a level that carries the scene, and use little music or none.
Keep the dialogue under 10 lines in a scene and let a pause run 5 to 15 s.
anti_patterns: Fast cutting under 5 s average shot length
A score that tells the viewer how to feel
A shot and reverse shot coverage of each line
An expository line that explains the plot
A hero with a clear goal and a finish
A cutaway that releases the tension of a long wait

composition.framing: A wide, level frame with the horizon at the lower or upper third; the person is small and the place is large.
composition.staging_in_depth: A deep, still space of 3 planes: a foreground edge, the person in the middle ground and a distant line of land or a wall.
composition.subject_placement: Small, off centre, often seen from behind or from the side; a figure walks into the depth along a diagonal or a straight line.

principles.rule: Leave most of the frame to the sky, the field or the room, and keep the person small in it.
Show the person at a small share of the frame height so that the place outweighs the figure.
Hold each shot well past its plot point, and cut only when the viewer's attention has settled.
Set the horizon on the lower or the upper third line, and the figure on a vertical third.
principles.value: horizon at 33% or 67% of the height

principles.rule: Keep the frame level and fixed, with no cut-in, for the whole of a scene.
principles.value: 0 cut-ins in a scene, locked off for 90% or more of the shots

camera_and_movement.movement: Locked-off for most shots. A slow track or a pan, at 0.2 to 0.5 m/s, follows a person through a space, or a long push-in over 60 to 120 s.
camera_and_movement.support: Tripod or a slow dolly; a long-take rig on a car or a track
camera_and_movement.camera_height: 1.2 to 1.6 m, eye level; a low tripod at 0.8 m in a field
camera_and_movement.move_speed: Track 0.2 to 0.5 m/s; pan 2° to 5° per second

lens_and_format.focal_length: 28mm to 50mm (35mm format); a wide lens for a long shot
lens_and_format.aperture: f/5.6 to f/11 for deep focus
lens_and_format.resolution: 35mm negative, 16mm or 4K digital; scan at 2K or 4K
lens_and_format.focus: Deep focus: the person, the room and the far land are all readable.

light.quality: Soft, natural and low in contrast, as the day and the weather give it; a lamp or a window in the frame.
light.direction: From the window or the sky; the light changes slowly in a long shot and is kept.
light.colour_temperature: Daylight 5600K, or a window and a tungsten lamp 3200K left uncorrected
light.source: The sun, the sky, windows and practical lamps

colour_and_grade.treatment: A natural, muted colour or black and white. Greys and earth tones; no stylised grade, and the light is allowed to change.
grade_recipe: Set the black point at 4% and the white point at 94% with a gentle contrast of +5%.
Keep saturation at 80% to 90% of the original; do not tint.
Hold the skin at the natural 12% to 14% to the vectorscope skin line.
Add grain at 8% to 12% to match 16mm or 35mm.
Do not add a vignette, a flare or a LUT.
colour_and_grade.texture: Fine grain at 8% to 12%, with natural noise in the dark

editing_and_rhythm.average_shot_length: 30 to 180 s (Sátántangó is reported at about 150 shots in 7 h, check Cinemetrics for each title)
editing_and_rhythm.shot_length_range: 10 s for a short shot to 10 min for a long take
editing_and_rhythm.cutting_logic: Cut only to change the place or the time. Let the action run out, and hold the empty frame for 3 to 10 s after the person has left.
editing_and_rhythm.transitions: Hard cut, a long fade of 2 to 4 s to black and no effect.

sound.approach: The sound of the place at its real level, with wind, rain, an engine, a clock, and an off-screen voice.
sound.dialogue: Sparse and flat, fewer than 10 lines in a scene, with pauses of 5 to 15 s.
sound.music: Almost none: one diegetic song or a low drone, used once or twice in the whole film.
sound.loudness: −26 to −23 LUFS integrated, with a wide dynamic range

titles_and_graphics.treatment: A bare title card in white on black, a short credit list; subtitles in a plain white sans-serif.
titles_and_graphics.type: A plain sans-serif or serif in white lower case, 4 to 6 s for the title.

shot_primer.opening: Open on a wide, still shot of a landscape or a room and let it run 60 s or more before a person enters.

positive: ordinary person in a vast landscape

canonical_works.work: Jeanne Dielman, 23 quai du Commerce, 1080 Bruxelles
Uncle Boonmee Who Can Recall His Past Lives

emotion.target_response: Stillness and attention: the viewer slows down, notices small things and feels time as a weight.

use_cases: video prompts for a quiet scene
avoid_when: The piece must hold a viewer under 15 s on a feed.
The brief needs a clear plot, a hook or a call to action.

modifiers.how: Keep the wide frame and the single take; add a choreographed fight or a chase inside the take, with a move of 1 to 3 m/s.
Keep the long take and the sound of the place; drop the staging, shoot handheld on location and let the subject address the camera.

sources.title: Matthew Flanagan, Towards an Aesthetic of Slow in Contemporary Cinema (16:9, 2008)
Tiago de Luca and Nuno Barradas Jorge (eds.), Slow Cinema (Edinburgh University Press, 2016)
